lines.text: Most people do not lose money in the stock market because they picked the wrong stock. They lose it because of a handful of simple mistakes.
Mistakes that are easy to make, hard to notice, and very expensive. Today I show you the five biggest ones, with real numbers.
And at the end, I will show you the boring habit that protects you from almost all of them.
A quick note first: this video is for education only. It is not financial advice.
Phase one: the real enemy.
Over the very long run, the S&P 500, an index of about five hundred big American companies, has returned roughly ten percent per year on average, before inflation.

spec.label: per year, long-run average
spec.sub: S&P 500, before inflation. An average, not a promise.

lines.text: But that is the return of the market. Many studies find that the typical investor earns less than the funds they own, because of badly timed decisions.
The good news: these mistakes are well known, and avoiding them costs nothing. So let us go through the five, one by one.
Phase two: money you need soon.
Mistake number one: investing money you will need within the next few years. Rent, tuition, a car, a down payment, or an emergency.
The stock market tends to rise over the long run. But in the short run it can fall hard, and it does not care about your deadlines.
Look at the crash of two thousand eight. From its peak in October two thousand seven to its low in March two thousand nine, the S&P 500 fell almost fifty-seven percent.
It then took until March two thousand thirteen, more than five years, just to get back to the old peak.
Imagine you put in twenty thousand dollars in October two thousand seven. At the bottom, it would have been worth only about eighty-six hundred dollars.
A common rule of thumb: money you need within a few years does not belong in stocks. It belongs in boring places, like a savings account.

Many experts suggest an emergency fund of three to six months of living costs. Yet in a Federal Reserve survey, only sixty-three percent of adults said they could cover a four hundred dollar emergency with cash.

spec.title: Could cover a $400 emergency with cash?

lines.text: Why does that matter for investing? Because without a cushion, a car repair can force you to sell your stocks at the worst possible moment, in the middle of a crash.
Phase three: borrowing and gambling.
Mistake number two: investing with borrowed money, or treating the market like a casino.
Start with credit cards. The average card charges about twenty-one percent interest per year, according to Federal Reserve data from May two thousand twenty-six.
So if you invest money you borrowed on a card, your investments would have to beat twenty-one percent every single year, just to break even.
Then there is leverage, which means investing with money borrowed from your broker. It sounds smart, but it works in both directions.
Say you put in ten thousand dollars of your own money, and borrow another ten thousand. Now you control twenty thousand dollars of stocks.

The market drops twenty-five percent. Your stocks are now worth fifteen thousand. But you still owe ten thousand, so you are left with five thousand. A twenty-five percent drop just cost you half of your money.
And if the market falls fifty percent, like in two thousand eight, you are wiped out completely. Often the broker sells your stocks even earlier, in what is called a margin call.

Next, daily trading. A study followed almost twenty thousand new day traders in Brazil, from two thousand thirteen to two thousand fifteen. Of those who lasted at least three hundred days, ninety-seven percent lost money.
Only about one percent earned more than the local minimum wage. That is not a reason to feel stupid. It is a reason to be careful, because you are trading against professionals with fast computers.
And meme coins and hot tips? If something can double in a week, it can also lose ninety percent in a week. Never use money you cannot afford to lose completely.
Phase four: the fee trap.
Mistake number three: ignoring fees. A one percent fee sounds like nothing. It is not nothing.
Let us do the math. Ten thousand dollars, invested for thirty years at a market return of seven percent per year, becomes about seventy-six thousand dollars.
Now take away a one percent yearly fee. At six percent, the same ten thousand dollars becomes only about fifty-seven thousand dollars.
That is almost nineteen thousand dollars lost to fees. About a quarter of your final amount, from just one percent per year.

What do funds really cost? In two thousand twenty-four, the average equity mutual fund in the United States charged about zero point four percent per year. Index ETFs, which simply track a market, averaged only about zero point one four percent.

And expensive active funds promise to beat the market. Most do not. According to the S&P SPIVA report, almost ninety percent of active large-cap US funds underperformed the S&P 500 over the fifteen years to the end of two thousand twenty-four.

spec.title: Active US large-cap funds vs. S&P 500, 15 years
spec.foot: S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA, Dec 2024

lines.text: The fix is free: before you buy any fund, look up its expense ratio. If it costs several times more than a simple index fund, it needs to give you something very special for that price.
Phase five: panic and timing.
Mistake number four: selling in a panic, or trying to time the market. When prices fall, every instinct says: get out. And that feels safe.
But selling after a crash turns a temporary loss into a permanent one. You lock in the loss, and you often miss the recovery, which starts while the news is still terrible.

Here is the proof. J.P. Morgan looked at the twenty years from two thousand five to two thousand twenty-four. Someone who stayed fully invested in the S&P 500 earned about ten point four percent per year. Ten thousand dollars grew to roughly seventy-two thousand.

Now imagine you missed only the ten best days, out of about five thousand trading days. Your return falls to about six percent per year, and your ten thousand grows to only about thirty-three thousand.
Miss the twenty best days, and you earn about three point six percent per year. Miss the thirty best days, and it is only about one point four percent.
And here is the cruel part. Seven of the ten best days came within two weeks of one of the ten worst days. The investor who runs away after the crash is often the one who misses the rebound.

spec.label: best days
spec.sub: came within two weeks of one of the 10 worst days. S&P 500, 2005–2024 (J.P. Morgan)

lines.text: A simple trick: write down your plan while the market is calm. Then, when it crashes, you do not have to decide anything. You just follow the plan.
Phase six: one stock, one hype.
Mistake number five: putting everything on one stock, one sector, or one hype. It feels exciting when it works. It is brutal when it does not.
Even great companies can lose most of their value, and some go to zero. Enron and Lehman Brothers were both giants, and both ended in bankruptcy.

Now the surprising part. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder studied almost twenty-six thousand US stocks from nineteen twenty-six to twenty sixteen. Only about four percent of them created all of the net wealth above Treasury bills.
Fifty-eight percent of stocks did not even beat Treasury bills over their lifetimes.
So picking one stock means betting that you found one of the rare winners. Owning many stocks means you own the winners automatically, even if you cannot name them in advance.

That is what diversification means. Not a fancy trick, just spreading your money across hundreds or thousands of companies, ideally across industries and countries. A broad index fund does that in a single purchase.
Be careful with tips on social media, too. The person on screen may be paid to promote something, may already own the stock, and you rarely see their losing trades.
A simple test: if someone says it is guaranteed, urgent, or a secret, walk away. Real investing is slow, public, and a little bit boring.
Phase seven: what they have in common.
Look at the five together. Money you need soon, borrowed money, high fees, panic selling, and all-in bets. They look different, but they share one thing.
And none of them is about intelligence. Smart people make these mistakes all the time, because they are driven by emotions: fear, greed, and the fear of missing out.
Phase eight: the boring plan.
So what do people do instead? Here is what many educational sources suggest, not advice for you personally. First: build an emergency fund, and pay off expensive debt.
Second: money for the long term, ten years or more, often goes into low-cost, broadly diversified funds.
Third: invest regularly, for example every month, so you never have to guess the perfect moment.
Fourth: write down your plan, and check your portfolio rarely. Looking at it every day mostly makes you nervous.
And fifth: keep learning, and be honest about what you do not know. If your situation is complicated, a licensed advisor can help.
None of this is exciting. And that is the point. Boring is what makes it work.
Phase nine: the honest answer.

So, what should you never do with your money when you invest? Never invest money you need soon. Never invest borrowed money or gamble. Never ignore fees. Never panic sell. And never put everything on one stock or one hype.
Will avoiding them make you rich quickly? No. There are no guarantees in investing, and markets can still fall. But you give yourself the best chance, because you stay in the game.
Remember, this video is for education only. It is not financial advice. I do not know your situation or your goals, so do your own research, or talk to a licensed professional.
Now tell me in the comments: which of these five mistakes have you seen most often, or made yourself? No judgment. Everyone starts somewhere.
And subscribe for more honest money math. In the next video, we look at what a small monthly amount turns into over thirty years.
